title: CUET Mass Media Test 12
subject: Mass Media / Mass Communication (Code: 318)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Mass Media - 318.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Mass Media papers 2024, 2025 and 2026, analysed for format only (no questions copied)
textbooks: CBSE Mass Media Studies, Classes XI-XII (curriculum mirrored by the NTA syllabus)
Constitution of India, Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(2); Acts and Supreme Court judgments as cited
Official histories of All India Radio, Doordarshan and Indian cinema
instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
One set of 5 questions is based on a case; the set stays together.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.sub_topic: Free basic service with paid extras
questions.question: A news app that offers most stories free but charges for in-depth articles and an ad-free version follows a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Freemium model
Why: Freemium gives basic content free and charges for premium features.
Why not the others: (A) is funded by the state for all. (C) ignores digital. (D) is owned by members.
Key point: Digital media are still searching for ways to make money.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.question: Organisations such as Reuters and the Associated Press that supply photographs to many newspapers are called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Photo agencies
Why: Photo agencies employ photographers and sell their pictures to many media outlets.
Why not the others: (A) make advertisements. (B) regulate the press. (C) screen films.
Key point: Agencies let papers carry pictures from around the world.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.question: In the AIDA model, the letter "D" stands for ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Desire
Why: AIDA stands for Attention, Interest, Desire and Action.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are not part of the model.
Key point: An advertisement moves the buyer from attention to action.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.sub_topic: Spelling hard names as they sound
questions.question: In a radio script, a difficult name is written as it sounds, for example "Thiruvananthapuram (thi-ru-va-nan-tha-pu-ram)". This is done so that:
options: B) Listeners can read it later
C) The name can be printed in a newspaper
D) The presenter pronounces it correctly
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The presenter pronounces it correctly
Why: Phonetic spelling helps the presenter say difficult names correctly on air.
Why not the others: (A) is not a purpose. (B) and (C) are wrong; listeners do not see the script.
Key point: Mispronouncing names hurts a station's credibility.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Part)
(A) Headline
(B) Body copy
(C) Call to action
(D) Visual

List-II (Role)
(I) Tells the reader what to do, such as "Order today"
(II) Gives the details and benefits of the product
(III) The picture that catches the eye
(IV) The top line that grabs attention
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: The headline grabs attention (IV). The body copy gives details (II). The call to action tells the reader what to do (I), and the visual catches the eye (III).
Why not the others: (B) swaps headline and body copy. (C) swaps body copy and call to action. (D) swaps call to action and visual.
Key point: Each part of an advertisement has one job.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Fake news often uses shocking or emotional language.
(B) Checking the source and the date of a post helps detect fake news.
(C) Writing "forwarded as received" removes responsibility for spreading a false message.
(D) Fact-checking websites help users verify claims.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A), (B) and (D) are correct. Emotional language is a warning sign, checking source and date helps, and fact-checkers verify claims.
Why not the others: (C) is false. Whoever forwards a false message helps spread it, whatever note is added. Options (C) and (D) include (C), and (A) leaves out (D).
Key point: Every user shares responsibility for what they forward.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: A smaller group within a culture
questions.question: Fans of a music style who share their own slang, clothes and values within the wider society form a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Subculture
Why: A subculture is a group with its own distinct ways inside a larger culture.
Why not the others: (B) is a large scattered audience. (C) is a traditional form of performance. (D) is the space where citizens discuss public matters.
Key point: Media often spread and shape subcultures.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Technique)
(A) Cross-cutting
(B) Jump cut
(C) Match cut
(D) Flashback

List-II (Effect)
(I) Takes the story back to an earlier time
(II) Links two shots through a similar shape or movement
(III) Moves back and forth between two places where action is happening
(IV) An abrupt jump forward in time within the same shot
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: Cross-cutting moves between two places (III). A jump cut jumps forward abruptly (IV). A match cut links similar shapes (II), and a flashback goes back in time (I).
Why not the others: (B) swaps cross-cutting and jump cut. (C) swaps jump cut and match cut. (D) swaps match cut and flashback.
Key point: Editing controls time and space in a film.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: Why mass communication is called impersonal
questions.question: Mass communication is often called impersonal because:
options: A) It uses only written words and never pictures
B) It cannot carry any emotion to its audience
C) It is always paid for by the government
D) The sender does not know the receivers personally
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The sender does not know the receivers personally
Why: The sender addresses a large, unknown audience, not individuals they know.
Why not the others: (A) is false; it uses sound and pictures too. (B) is false; it can be very emotional. (C) is false; many media are private.
Key point: Mass communication speaks to many people, but not to anyone in particular.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question: Udant Martand, the first Hindi newspaper, was published in 1826 from ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Calcutta
Why: Udant Martand was published from Calcutta by Jugal Kishore Shukla.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) were not where it was published.
Key point: Calcutta was the early centre of the Indian press.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: What a TV script's audio column does not hold
questions.question: A TV script is often written in two columns, one for video and one for audio. Which of the following does NOT belong in the audio column?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Camera shot sizes
Why: Shot sizes describe the picture, so they go in the video column.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are all sounds and belong in the audio column.
Key point: The two-column script keeps picture and sound in step.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.sub_topic: A phone that runs apps and the internet
questions.question: A mobile phone that can use the internet and run apps is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Smartphone
Why: A smartphone combines a phone with internet access and apps.
Why not the others: (B) is a fixed phone line. (C) only received short messages. (D) is a two-way radio.
Key point: The smartphone is the main device of new media.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.question:
Arrange the following steps of a live phone-in programme in the correct order:
(A) The caller is put on air to speak
(B) The presenter sums up and closes the programme
(C) A producer screens the calls off air
(D) The presenter announces the topic and the phone number
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D), (C), (A), (B)
Why: The presenter announces the topic and number, the producer screens calls, callers go on air, and the presenter sums up at the end.
Why not the others: (A) screens calls before the number is given. (B) puts callers on air before screening. (C) closes the show before callers speak.
Key point: Screening keeps a live phone-in safe and on topic.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.question: Recorded moving pictures, before or after editing, are called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Footage
Why: Footage is the recorded video material.
Why not the others: (B) is the written text. (C) is drawings of shots. (D) is the order of items in a show.
Key point: Editors work with footage to build a programme.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.question: A radio programme in which the presenter plays songs that listeners have asked for is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Request show
Why: A request show plays music chosen by listeners, often with their messages.
Why not the others: (A) is built on conversation. (C) tells a story. (D) gives the news.
Key point: Request shows build a bond with listeners.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: An unusual event staged for coverage
questions.question: A company builds a giant model of its product in a city square so that newspapers and TV channels will cover it. This is a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Publicity stunt
Why: A publicity stunt is an eye-catching event designed to attract media coverage.
Why not the others: (A) is a written statement. (B) is a magazine for employees. (C) invites journalists to an event.
Key point: Stunts can win attention but may backfire if they seem silly.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.question: Online platforms can profit from many niche products, such as rare books or regional songs, that would never fill a shop shelf. This idea is called the:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Long tail
Why: The long tail describes how the internet makes it possible to serve many small, niche audiences.
Why not the others: (A) is McLuhan's world linked by media. (B) is the gap in access. (D) is hearing only one's own views.
Key point: The internet gives room to niche content.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question: Waving a hand to say goodbye is an example of a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Gesture
Why: A gesture is a movement of the body, such as a wave, that sends a message without words.
Why not the others: (A) uses written words. (C) reaches large audiences. (D) is not a term for a hand signal.
Key point: Gestures are part of non-verbal communication.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) All India Radio comes to be called Akashvani
(B) DD Kisan is launched
(C) Prasar Bharati comes into existence
(D) A television centre opens in Bombay
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (D), (C), (B)
Why: AIR came to be called Akashvani in 1957. The Bombay TV centre opened in 1972, Prasar Bharati was formed in 1997, and DD Kisan was launched in 2015.
Why not the others: (B) puts 1972 before 1957. (C) puts 1997 before 1972. (D) puts 2015 before 1997.
Key point: Public broadcasting grew over six decades.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: Types of press pictures by purpose
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Photograph)
(A) Spot news photo
(B) Feature photo
(C) Sports action photo
(D) Portrait

List-II (Description)
(I) A posed or planned picture showing a person's face and character
(II) Taken at an unplanned event as it happens
(III) Freezes a key moment in a game
(IV) A human-interest picture not tied to breaking news
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why: A spot news photo is taken as an event happens (II). A feature photo is human interest (IV). A sports action photo freezes a moment of play (III), and a portrait shows a person's face and character (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps spot news and feature. (B) swaps feature and sports. (D) swaps sports and portrait.
Key point: Different kinds of photographs serve different purposes.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about Prasar Bharati:
(A) It is India's autonomous public service broadcaster.
(B) It runs both All India Radio and Doordarshan.
(C) Its chief executive is elected by Parliament.
(D) It was set up under an Act of Parliament.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A), (B) and (D) are correct. Prasar Bharati was set up under the Prasar Bharati Act and runs AIR and Doordarshan.
Why not the others: (C) is false. Its chief executive is appointed on the recommendation of a selection committee, not elected by Parliament. Options (B) and (D) include (C), and (A) leaves out (D).
Key point: Prasar Bharati was meant to give public broadcasting independence from day-to-day government control.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.question:
Arrange the following steps of producing a photo story in the correct order:
(A) Research and plan the story
(B) Write the captions and arrange the sequence
(C) Select and edit the best pictures
(D) Shoot the pictures in the field
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (D), (C), (B)
Why: The photographer plans, shoots, selects the best pictures, and then writes captions and arranges them.
Why not the others: (B) shoots before planning. (C) selects before shooting. (D) writes captions before choosing pictures.
Key point: Selection is as important as shooting.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.sub_topic: A short delay on live calls
questions.question: Live phone-in programmes are often broadcast a few seconds late so that the producer can cut offensive remarks before they go on air. This is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Broadcast delay
Why: A broadcast delay gives the producer a few seconds to remove unsuitable content.
Why not the others: (B) lowers sound to silence. (C) blends two sounds. (D) is music under speech.
Key point: Live radio needs safeguards.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Medium)
(A) Newspaper
(B) Radio
(C) Television
(D) Internet

List-II (Main strength)
(I) Portable and reaches people who cannot read
(II) Lets users respond and create content
(III) A lasting record that can be read again
(IV) Combines moving pictures and sound
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: A newspaper can be kept and re-read (III). Radio is portable and needs no reading (I). TV combines pictures and sound (IV), and the internet is interactive (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps newspaper and radio. (B) swaps radio and TV. (C) swaps TV and internet.
Key point: Each medium has its own strengths.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: An advertisement strip on a website
questions.question: A rectangular advertisement across the top or side of a web page is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Banner ad
Why: A banner ad is a display advertisement placed on a web page.
Why not the others: (A) is a small text advertisement in a newspaper. (C) is an outdoor board. (D) is a short song.
Key point: Banner ads were among the first forms of online advertising.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: Dealing with issues before they become crises
questions.question: A company's PR team watches public concerns about plastic waste and acts early to change its packaging before criticism grows. This is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Issue management
Why: Issue management spots emerging concerns and deals with them before they turn into crises.
Why not the others: (A) responds once a crisis has broken. (B) purchases advertising space. (D) promotes banned products indirectly.
Key point: Preventing a crisis is better than managing one.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Data breach
(B) End-to-end encryption
(C) Privacy policy
(D) Geotag

List-II (Meaning)
(I) Only the sender and receiver can read the message
(II) Location information attached to a post or photo
(III) A document explaining how a service uses personal data
(IV) A leak of stored personal data to unauthorised people
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(II)
Why: A data breach leaks personal data (IV). End-to-end encryption lets only sender and receiver read messages (I). A privacy policy explains data use (III), and a geotag reveals location (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps breach and encryption. (B) swaps encryption and privacy policy. (C) swaps privacy policy and geotag.
Key point: Users should know how their data is protected and shared.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Piracy reduces the income of producers and everyone who worked on a film.
(B) The Cinematograph (Amendment) Act, 2023 made recording a film in a cinema without permission an offence.
(C) Piracy is legal once a film is more than a year old.
(D) Selling satellite and OTT rights is a source of income for films.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false. Copyright lasts for decades, so pirating an old film is still illegal.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are correct. Options (A), (C) and (D) name a correct statement as false.
Key point: Films earn from cinemas, TV, OTT and more, and piracy cuts into all of these.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.question: Setting screen-time limits and taking breaks from social media to protect one's health is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Digital wellbeing
Why: Digital wellbeing means using technology in a healthy, balanced way.
Why not the others: (B) is the gap in access. (C) is the trail a user leaves online. (D) is an electronic way of signing.
Key point: Balanced use protects mental health.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) In Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Supreme Court held that speech over the internet is protected under Article 19(1)(a).
(B) The Court said that internet shutdowns must be necessary and proportionate.
(C) The digital divide affects rural and poorer citizens more.
(D) Online speech in India is free of all restrictions.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false. Online speech is subject to the same reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) and to laws such as the IT Act.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are correct. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a correct statement as false.
Key point: The internet extends free speech, along with its limits.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: Papers used in planning a shoot
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Document)
(A) Shot list
(B) Shooting schedule
(C) Release form
(D) Treatment

List-II (Purpose)
(I) Lists every shot to be filmed
(II) Records the permission of people who appear on screen
(III) Sets out when and where each scene will be shot
(IV) Describes the programme in prose before the script
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV)
Why: A shot list lists every shot (I). A shooting schedule sets times and places (III). A release form records permission (II), and a treatment describes the programme in prose (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps shot list and schedule. (C) swaps schedule and release form. (D) swaps release form and treatment.
Key point: Careful paperwork makes a shoot run smoothly.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Programme)
(A) Mann Ki Baat
(B) Hawa Mahal
(C) Binaca Geetmala
(D) Yuv Vani

List-II (Description)
(I) A countdown of popular film songs
(II) The Prime Minister's monthly address on AIR
(III) Short radio plays on Vividh Bharati
(IV) AIR's programmes made by and for young people
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)
Why: Mann Ki Baat is the Prime Minister's monthly address (II). Hawa Mahal carries radio plays (III). Binaca Geetmala was a song countdown (I), and Yuv Vani is AIR's youth service (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps Mann Ki Baat and Hawa Mahal. (B) swaps Hawa Mahal and Binaca Geetmala. (D) swaps Binaca Geetmala and Yuv Vani.
Key point: Radio has served politics, drama, music and youth.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.sub_topic: When the censor board got its present name
questions.question: The Central Board of Film Censors was renamed the Central Board of Film Certification in:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1983
Why: The board was renamed in 1983, stressing certification rather than censorship.
Why not the others: (B) is the year of the Cinematograph Act. (C) and (D) are not the year of renaming.
Key point: The new name reflected the board's main task of classifying films.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about audience research:
(A) Audience research is done only after a programme has been cancelled.
(B) Channels use audience research to plan programmes.
(C) Focus groups give detailed opinions from a small group of viewers.
(D) Social media gives channels quick feedback from viewers.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A) only
Why: Only (A) is false. Audience research is done before, during and after programmes to guide decisions.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are correct. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a correct statement as false.
Key point: Knowing the audience shapes every programme decision.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.question: People who appear in the background of crowd scenes without speaking roles are called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Junior artists (extras)
Why: Junior artists, or extras, fill crowd and background scenes.
Why not the others: (A) play main roles. (C) perform dangerous scenes. (D) provide voices.
Key point: Large productions employ many junior artists.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.question: A fraudster pretends to be from a company's IT department and persuades an employee to reveal her password. This is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Social engineering
Why: Social engineering manipulates people, rather than computers, into giving away information.
Why not the others: (A) guesses passwords by computer. (B) sends bulk messages. (C) provokes people online.
Key point: People are often the weakest link in security.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.sub_topic: A film meant to make people laugh
questions.question: A film whose main aim is to make the audience laugh belongs to the genre of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Comedy
Why: Comedy uses humour to entertain.
Why not the others: (A) aims to frighten. (B) builds suspense. (C) ends in suffering.
Key point: Genres are defined partly by the response they aim for.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: The one who pays for an advertisement
questions.question: The company that pays for an advertisement to promote its product is called the:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Advertiser
Why: The advertiser pays for the space or time and decides what to promote.
Why not the others: (A) owns the medium. (B) buys the product. (D) supplies products to shops.
Key point: Advertisers are the main source of income for many media.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.question: A photograph a person takes of themselves, usually with a phone, is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Selfie
Why: A selfie is a self-portrait taken with a phone or camera.
Why not the others: (A) is usually taken by another person. (B) is a humorous image. (D) is a small preview image.
Key point: Selfies are a common form of social media content.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) Lagaan is nominated for the Oscar for best foreign-language film
(B) "Naatu Naatu" from RRR wins the Oscar for best original song
(C) Mother India is released
(D) Salaam Bombay! is released
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (D), (A), (B)
Why: Mother India was released in 1957 and Salaam Bombay! in 1988. Lagaan, released in 2001, was nominated the next year, and "Naatu Naatu" won in 2023.
Why not the others: (A) puts 1988 before 1957. (B) puts Lagaan before Salaam Bombay!. (D) puts 2023 before Lagaan.
Key point: Indian cinema has slowly won wider international recognition.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: Judging other cultures by one's own
questions.question: Believing that one's own culture is superior and judging others by its standards is a barrier to communication called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ethnocentrism
Why: Ethnocentrism makes people dismiss or misread messages from other cultures.
Why not the others: (A) comes from word meanings. (C) is a response. (D) is putting ideas into words.
Key point: Respect for other cultures improves communication.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.question: Charts, maps and diagrams that present numbers and information visually in a newspaper are called ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) infographics
Why: Infographics turn data into visual form so that it is easy to grasp.
Why not the others: (A) comment through drawings. (C) explain photos. (D) carry the paper's name.
Key point: Infographics help readers understand complex numbers.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Advertising space is paid for, while PR coverage is earned.
(B) The advertiser controls the message, while in PR the media decide what to publish.
(C) Coverage earned through PR is often seen as more credible than an advertisement.
(D) PR and advertising can never be used together in one campaign.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are correct. Advertising is paid and controlled; PR coverage is earned and judged by the media, which makes it more credible.
Why not the others: (D) is false. Most campaigns combine PR and advertising. Options (B) and (C) include (D), and (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: PR and advertising work best together.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: Not part of Shannon and Weaver's model
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an element of Shannon and Weaver's model?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Opinion leader
Why: The opinion leader belongs to studies of how media influence spreads through people. Shannon and Weaver's model has a source, transmitter, channel, receiver, destination and noise.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are elements of the model.
Key point: Shannon and Weaver's model is a technical one.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.question: The running numbers recorded on video, showing hours, minutes, seconds and frames, which help editors find any moment exactly, are called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Time code
Why: Time code gives every frame a unique address for precise editing.
Why not the others: (A) is the shape of the frame. (B) is frames per second. (D) is the amount of data per second.
Key point: Time code makes editing and logging precise.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: A set of pictures that tells one story
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

When several factories in an industrial town shut down suddenly, thousands of migrant workers begin walking to their villages, hundreds of kilometres away. Meera, a photojournalist, travels with one group for four days.

Her paper publishes twelve of her pictures over two pages as a single story of the journey. It opens with a wide shot of a long line of walkers on an empty highway, followed by close-ups of blistered feet, a mother carrying a sleeping child and a man sharing his last roti. Under each picture is a short text giving the person's name (used with their permission), the place and what is happening. For the picture of the child, Meera chose a frame in which the child's face cannot be seen.

While laying out the page, an editor suggests cropping a police van out of one picture "to make it look cleaner". Meera refuses, saying the van, which was stopping walkers at a district border, is part of the story. None of the pictures was posed.

Question: Meera's twelve pictures, published together to tell the story of the journey, form a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Photo essay
Why: A photo essay is a series of photographs arranged to tell one story.
Why not the others: (A) is the text under a picture. (C) is a set of drawings. (D) is one picture with one story.
Key point: A photo essay has a beginning, a middle and an end, like a written story.

Her paper publishes twelve of her pictures over two pages as a single story of the journey. Under each picture is a short text giving the person's name (used with their permission), the place and what is happening. For the picture of the child, Meera chose a frame in which the child's face cannot be seen.

While laying out the page, an editor suggests cropping a police van out of one picture "to make it look cleaner". Meera refuses, saying the van, which was stopping walkers at a district border, is part of the story. None of the pictures was posed.

Question: The short text under each picture, naming the person, the place and what is happening, shows that a good caption should:
options: A) Express the photographer's opinion of the scene
B) Repeat the headline of the story word for word
C) Describe the camera and lens settings used
D) Identify who is shown, where, and what is happening
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Identify who is shown, where, and what is happening
Why: A caption tells readers who is in the picture, where it was taken and what is happening, so that the image can be understood correctly.
Why not the others: (A) is not the job of a news caption. (B) adds nothing. (C) is technical detail that readers do not need.
Key point: Captions turn a picture into information.

questions.sub_topic: Names used with permission and the child's face hidden
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

When several factories in an industrial town shut down suddenly, thousands of migrant workers begin walking to their villages, hundreds of kilometres away. Meera, a photojournalist, travels with one group for four days.

Her paper publishes twelve of her pictures over two pages as a single story of the journey. It opens with a wide shot of a long line of walkers on an empty highway, followed by close-ups of blistered feet, a mother carrying a sleeping child and a man sharing his last roti. Under each picture is a short text giving the person's name (used with their permission), the place and what is happening. For the picture of the child, Meera chose a frame in which the child's face cannot be seen.

While laying out the page, an editor suggests cropping a police van out of one picture "to make it look cleaner". Meera refuses, saying the van, which was stopping walkers at a district border, is part of the story. None of the pictures was posed.

Question: Meera used names only with permission and chose a frame that hid the child's face. These choices reflect the ethical principle of:
options: A) Respecting the privacy and dignity of vulnerable people
B) Making the pictures more dramatic for readers
C) Reducing the space the pictures take on the page
D) Avoiding copyright problems with the newspaper
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Respecting the privacy and dignity of vulnerable people
Why: Workers in distress and children are vulnerable. Seeking consent and protecting a child's identity respect their privacy and dignity.
Why not the others: (B) and (C) are not the reasons given. (D) is unrelated, since Meera took the pictures herself.
Key point: Photojournalists must weigh the story against the subjects' dignity.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: Why Meera refused to crop out the van
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

When several factories in an industrial town shut down suddenly, thousands of migrant workers begin walking to their villages, hundreds of kilometres away. Meera, a photojournalist, travels with one group for four days.

Her paper publishes twelve of her pictures over two pages as a single story of the journey. It opens with a wide shot of a long line of walkers on an empty highway, followed by close-ups of blistered feet, a mother carrying a sleeping child and a man sharing his last roti. Under each picture is a short text giving the person's name (used with their permission), the place and what is happening. For the picture of the child, Meera chose a frame in which the child's face cannot be seen.

While laying out the page, an editor suggests cropping a police van out of one picture "to make it look cleaner". Meera refuses, saying the van, which was stopping walkers at a district border, is part of the story. None of the pictures was posed.

Question: Why was Meera right to refuse to crop the police van out of the picture?
options: A) Newspapers are not allowed to crop any photograph
B) The van made the picture more colourful
C) Removing it would change what the picture tells readers
D) Police vehicles must always appear in news photos
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Removing it would change what the picture tells readers
Why: The van was stopping walkers at the border, so it was part of the story. Cropping it out would change the picture's meaning and mislead readers.
Why not the others: (A) is false; cropping for size is normal. (B) and (D) are not the reasons.
Key point: Editing a news photo must not change its meaning.

questions.sub_topic: Why the essay opens wide and then goes close
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

When several factories in an industrial town shut down suddenly, thousands of migrant workers begin walking to their villages, hundreds of kilometres away. Meera, a photojournalist, travels with one group for four days.

Her paper publishes twelve of her pictures over two pages as a single story of the journey. It opens with a wide shot of a long line of walkers on an empty highway, followed by close-ups of blistered feet, a mother carrying a sleeping child and a man sharing his last roti. Under each picture is a short text giving the person's name (used with their permission), the place and what is happening. For the picture of the child, Meera chose a frame in which the child's face cannot be seen.

While laying out the page, an editor suggests cropping a police van out of one picture "to make it look cleaner". Meera refuses, saying the van, which was stopping walkers at a district border, is part of the story. None of the pictures was posed.

Question: Why does the photo essay open with a wide shot of the highway before moving to close-ups?
options: A) Wide shots are cheaper to print than close-ups on newsprint
B) The wide shot shows the scale; the close-ups show human feeling
C) Close-ups matter less, so editors always place them later
D) Readers cannot understand any close-up printed without colour
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The wide shot shows the scale; the close-ups show human feeling
Why: The wide shot sets the scene and shows how many people are walking. The close-ups then bring readers near to individual suffering and kindness.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) are false. (C) is wrong; the close-ups carry much of the story's emotion.
Key point: Visual stories combine context and closeness.
